links.outcome: GPT-4o diagnostic sensitivity/specificity across three prompt variants (prevalence cues, removed category constraints)
links.effect: Baseline sensitivity 79.3%, specificity 45.2%; prevalence cues 30.4%/83.0%; no diagnostic categories 8.8%/94.7%. Performance highly sensitive to prompt variation.
links.quote: Baseline prompt (with diagnostic categories) achieved the highest sensitivity (79.3%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 73.4–84.1) with low specificity (45.2%, 95% CI 39.5–51.1), reflecting frequent over-calling of emergent conditions.

links.outcome: LLM diagnostic performance in stepwise simulation with real ED data versus static vignette expectations
links.effect: In simulated stepwise setting with real data, GPT-4o over-predicted rare conditions (sensitivity 79.3%, specificity 45.2%) and diverged from physicians and BN-optimal pathways (RBO 0.060-0.097).
links.quote: The relatively low diagnostic accuracy we observed may partly reflect this closer adherence to real-world complexity.

links.outcome: LLM calibration to realistic disease prevalence of life-threatening diagnoses
links.effect: GPT-4o over-selected rare life-threatening diagnoses at baseline (specificity 45.2%, 155 false positives of 283 non-emergent); prevalence cues tempered but did not eliminate the bias.
links.quote: This heterogeneity presents a more authentic calibration challenge, exposing the LLM’s tendency to over-select “zebra” diagnoses even when true prevalence information was provided.

links.outcome: Accuracy of LLM differential/diagnosis selection for emergent chest pain conditions
links.effect: Baseline over-called emergent conditions (specificity 45.2%); with prevalence cues or no categories, sensitivity fell to 30.4% and 8.8%, missing emergent diagnoses.
links.quote: With baseline prompting, GPT-4o systematically over-predicted rare conditions (sensitivity 79.3%; specificity 45.2%); adding prevalence cues or removing diagnostic category constraints respectively increased specificity (83.0% and 94.7%) while reducing false alarms by 107 and 140 per 500, but at the cost of poor sensitivity (30.4% and 8.8%).

links.outcome: Suitability of LLM diagnostic output for autonomous use
links.effect: Configuration miscalibrated and not suitable for clinical deployment; authors support cautious stance against autonomous diagnostic use and recommend clinician oversight.
links.quote: More broadly, our findings suggest that current diagnostic LLMs remain highly sensitive to prompt context and struggle with real-world clinical probabilities, supporting a cautious stance toward autonomous or patient-facing diagnostic use.
